title: Sales rebuttals and migration triggers — LLM API competitors
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, field-friendly playbook for reps and AE/SE pairs when facing other LLM API providers. Focus: short rebuttals, migration triggers, and the specific feature traps customers often cite. Use as a living doc — update after every loss win to capture new objections and competitor moves.

Quick summary:
- Position Redwood as the inference-first partner: not just model access but predictable latency, cost controls, and private/dedicated options for regulated workloads.
- Talk about economics (tokens/sec, effective cost per useful request) not just price per token.
- Emphasize observable SLOs + rollback/fallback policies — this is the easier win vs providers that only expose a simple endpoint.

Competitor landscape (how customers describe them):
- Vendor A (large model-access provider): "Cheaper access to newest models, but variable latency and opaque queuing."
- Vendor B (ML infra vendor): "Good for self-hosting, lacks turnkey private control plane and enterprise rollouts."
- Vendor C (specialized embeddings/semantic search provider): "Strong embedding quality, limited runtime controls and no dedicated GPU pools."
- Typical customer perception: speed-to-prototype vs speed-to-production are different buying motions.

Feature comparison notes (talking points, not a brute-force matrix):
- Hosted API: competitor wins on immediate model freshness; rebuttal: freshness alone doesn't solve tail latency, cost, or compliance. Offer: free POC + latency profile report.
- Dedicated capacity & SLAs: Redwood differentiator — explain how reserved pools, burst policies, and explicit latency targets reduce jitter. Rebuttal to "we can reserve IP ourselves": ask about team bandwidth to tune batching, cache, and kernel selection across model versions.
- Private/VPC deployments: competitors may claim "bring-your-model" flexibility; emphasize Redwood's private control plane + lifecycle tooling (pin versions, rollouts) that reduces ops lift.
- Observability & cost attribution: Redwood gives token-level cost and per-route breakdowns. If competitor says "we have logs": ask for token breakdown & trace-to-cost mapping.
- Quality monitoring & rollback: Redwood links evals to rollouts. If a customer worries about hallucinations, highlight canary evals and automatic fallback to a more conservative model variant.
- Performance tooling (batching/caching, quantization recommendations): competitor gap: many expose model configs but not intelligent workload-driven recommendations.

Common traps and how to avoid them (for sales):
- Trap: Over-indexing on headline model performance.
  Response: "Great — what are your 95th/99th latency goals, and how many concurrent requests do you expect? We measure real workload latency under your token distribution."
- Trap: Pricing comparison that ignores batching/caching and effective throughput.
  Response: "If we normalize for effective requests/min and cache hit rates we'll often show 20–50% lower spend at equal quality. We can run a quick cost-model with your sample traffic."
- Trap: "We already host models in-house."
  Response: "Ok — what's your SRE bandwidth for tuning kernels, continuous batching, and KV caching? Many teams realize the ops tax is > the marginal infra cost. We offer dedicated mode to offload that."
- Trap: "We need the absolute latest model; can't be pinned."
  Response: "We support both: you can point some routes at bleeding-edge hosted models while keeping critical routes on pinned, vetted releases with rollbacks and eval gates."

Short objection-handling scripts (copyable):
- Objection: "Your per-token price is higher."
  Script: "Two-minute ask: give me one day's typical traffic or sample prompts and we’ll run a cost comparison — including caching and batching effects. We typically find the unit cost story flips once you include production controls and hit rates."
- Objection: "Latency is unacceptable compared to Vendor A."
  Script: "When do you see spikes? We’ll instrument a 48-hour synthetic run on your sequence lengths and deliver a 95/99th latency profile; we can also show how dedicated capacity smooths those spikes."
- Objection: "Security/compliance — we need air-gapped/on-prem."
  Script: "We have Private deployments with optional air-gap packaging and KMS/HSM integrations. We can map your controls to our checklist and produce a gap plan in a week."

Discovery probe questions (to reveal migration triggers):
- What percent of requests must meet Xms latency (p50/p95/p99)?
- How often do you see quality regressions after model updates?
- Do you need per-tenant cost attribution or per-route SLOs?
- How many models/versions do you expect to serve concurrently?
- What internal SRE/infra bandwidth do you have for continuous tuning?

Signals that indicate a high-propensity migration: (use in qualification)
- Regular production incidents after model upgrades (quality or latency).
- Unclear cost attribution across teams or routes.
- Regulatory/compliance needs (SOC2/ISO) + desire for VPC/on-prem.
- Spikey traffic with hard tail-latency SLAs.

Call cheats (memorize these 6 lines):
1) "We don't just host models — we make inference predictable and cheap at scale."
2) "Dedicated pools + automatic fallback = fewer outages during traffic spikes."
3) "Token-level cost + per-route metrics mean you can optimize team-level budgets."
4) "Private deployment option for regulated data with the same console/rollouts."
5) "We tie evals to rollouts so quality regressions get caught before they ship."
6) "Let us run a 48-hour traffic replay and cost-latency model — no commitment."

Competitive play examples (short stories to tell):
- Migration case: fintech customer had intermittent p99 spikes and opaque queuing with Vendor A. After a 2-week Dedicated POC, p99 dropped 40%, and cost per useful request dropped 22% due to KV caching and smaller model variants for low-risk routes.
- On-prem case: regulated healthcare org needed private control plane but wanted the same rollout UX. Redwood delivered private control plane + canary evals; customer avoided an internal six-month infra project.

- Add one-pager with concrete cost-model template for AE to send to customers (include sample spreadsheet). Owner: Noah. Due: 2026-02-28.
- Capture 3 recent losses and extract new rebuttals. Owner: Aria. Due: ongoing.

Notes to self / field tips:
- Avoid overpromising on model-level accuracy vs base provider claims; pivot to operational risk and mitigation.
- Use customer prompts for POC — it's the single best way to expose latency/cost differences.
- When in doubt, offer a short controlled POC: 2–4 weeks, limited routes, clear success metrics.

End — keep this short doc as the AE cheat-sheet. Update after each competitive call with a quick line on which rebuttals worked.
